newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Northport sees exit from NZ engineering.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Northport sees exit from NZ engineering.

text.p: Northland Port Corp Ltd plans eventually to exit its marine engineering business to focus on its three remaining operations, Chief Executive Terry Archer said in a recent interview.

Archer told Reuters that the eventual departure would help guarantee the future of the Port of Whangarei while the company prepared to shift operations to a new NZ$50 million deepwater port planned for Marsden Point.
"While we are actively involved in marine engineering at the moment, that probably will not always be the case," Archer said.
Archer said Northland Port saw itself as a catalyst for getting marine engineering re-established in Whangarei, but expected a bigger operator to eventually take its place.
Looking ahead, Archer saw Northland Port's business as being in cargo and materials handling, shipping services and coastal transport in the form of Seatow.

Archer said Seatow, a tug and barge operation, had big potential, particularly on the South Island's West Coast, where port access is limited by sand bars, and the heavily afforested Far North, where road and sea access is often difficult.
"We basically have put our money on tug and barge operations because with a barge you've got a shallow draft and you can get big tonnages out of those harbours quite safely," Archer said.
Archer said shipbuilding was on the up and up in Whangarei, having attracted Australia's Transfield, the company making modules for the ANZAC Frigate project.
Northland Port is more diversified than most port utilities, a strategy that was borne from an over-reliance on the oil industry in the late 1980s.
When Whangarei Engineering collapsed, Northland Port bought its assets and melded them into its own.
"It's succeeded and since then we have expanded to the extent that we now probably turn over over NZ$30-35 million just out of marine engineering," he said.

The oil sector is still Northland Port's biggest customer but not nearly as big proportionately. Oil once represented about NZ10 million of its $12 million turnover but now makes up $12 million out of a total of $70 million.
Archer said Marsden Point had a comparative advantage for handling high volume commodities and liquids.
"Our whole group philosophy is built around these bulk homogenous cargoes and that applies to Seatow as well," he said.
As early as 1983, Archer said, studies showed the Port of Whangarei would not be able to handle the projected forestry volume from the region, obviating the need for another port.
Marsden Point was chosen for its proximity to Auckland, and directors envisaged it would become an overflow point for Auckland as that port became less involved in bulk cargo.
Archer expects the ownership of New Zealand's 13 port companies to be rationalised in the years to come and there were there already signs of cooperation between non-competing ports.
Northland Port is 72 percent-owned by the Northland Regional Council. The rest is owned by institutions and individuals.
